title: APC Network Management Card SNMP Communication Loss
exclusions: Sites that refuse SNMP toward APC cards, environments monitored solely through local serial consoles without Splunk ingest, or racks whose power gear never exposes PowerNet-MIB upsCommStatus to Splunk collectors.
evidence: Scheduled saved search archive of hosts whose latest upsCommStatus equals 2, exported weekly to the restricted facilities evidence library with Splunk audit fields (_time, host, mgmt_ip) retained for 400 days.

implementation: Baseline every APC firmware train because upsCommStatus enumerations occasionally shift between maintenance releases—promote lookups only after snmpget proof. When traps are sparse, dual-path ingest (poll + trap) prevents silent gaps if UDP traps drop during congestion. Pair Splunk alerts with ICMP tests sourced from two subnets so asymmetric routing failures do not masquerade as dead UPS hardware.

1. **Maintenance window on `power` (UC-15.1.29)** — Planned work for 'APC Network Management Card SNMP Communication Loss' shifts `count` over `span=1h` while `host` remains in-scope.  Cross-check CMDB CHG.

2. **Batch `count` on `snmp:apc:ups`** — Scheduled automation elevates `comm` without crossing configured threshold for UC-15.1.29. Compare `_time` minute against the job schedule.

4. **Onboarding burst for `snmp:apc:ups`** — First 48h baseline for UC-15.1.29 on `host` is unstable; window via `ops_exception_register.csv`.

detailedImplementation:
Prerequisites
• Deploy Splunk Connect for SNMP (Splunkbase #6266) workers or configure the SNMP Modular Input (Splunkbase #1537) on a Heavy Forwarder that can reach UDP/161 to each APC Network Management Card; confirm RBAC so splunkd can reload inputs—typically admin on Enterprise or sc_admin approvals on Splunk Cloud before publishing HEC or modular-input secrets.
• Reserve index=power (or your contracted SNMP landing index) and enforce props/transforms so sourcetype=snmp:apc:ups retains upsCommStatus as a numeric field; mirror trap ingest for APC enterprise OID .1.3.6.1.4.1.318 into sourcetype=snmp:trap when polls alone would miss asynchronous communicationLost events.
• Poll upsCommStatus at least every five minutes and document the OID-to-integer mapping per firmware family (commonly 1=ok, 2=commLost on classic builds).

Configuration steps
1. From a bastion host run snmpwalk/snmpget against a pilot UPS to capture live upsCommStatus samples; stash the proof in change records before Splunk alerting goes live.
2. Validate modular inputs via REST GET /services/data/inputs/snmp (or the equivalent SC4SNMP inventory UI) so each mgmt_ip maps to the intended sourcetype=snmp:apc:ups stanza without duplicate community strings shadowing each other.
3. Layer NetOps correlation: join hosts that flip upsCommStatus=2 with recent interfaceDown or firewall-change knowledge objects so VLAN ACL regressions separate from dead NMC hardware.
4. Tune scheduled searches with dispatch.earliest_time=-15m and three consecutive poll failures before paging to absorb transient SNMP timeouts during brief spanning-tree reconvergence.
5. Stand up a redundant poller host so scheduled maintenance on one collector never marks every UPS commLost simultaneously.

Operational follow-through
• Normalize odd string extractions using case() when legacy TA versions emit textual status tokens.
• Capture weekly CSV snapshots from the comm-loss saved search into the facilities evidence share for audit replay.

Step 1 — Configure data collection

Install and configure the upstream Splunk app or TA: Splunk Connect for SNMP (Splunkbase #6266), SNMP Modular Input (Splunkbase #1537).

**Expected data sources:** Requires Splunk Connect for SNMP (Splunkbase #6266) or the SNMP Modular Input add-on (Splunkbase #1537). Primary poll metrics arrive as sourcetype=snmp:apc:ups with the extracted numeric field upsCommStatus from PowerNet-MIB; complementary APC enterprise SNMP traps may appear under sourcetype=snmp:trap carrying communicationLost semantics for the same hosts.

**Indexes referenced by the SPL:** `power`
**Sourcetypes referenced by the SPL:** `snmp:apc:ups`, `snmp:trap`

After enabling the input, confirm event arrival on a search head with:

```spl
index=* sourcetype="snmp:apc:ups" earliest=-15m | head 5
```

Tune the input's polling interval, batch size, and field extraction to match the volume and latency requirements of the alert. Keep an operational baseline of expected events-per-minute so anomalous drops in ingest can be detected separately from anomalous behaviour.


Step 2 — Create the search and alert

Use the SPL on the use-case page as the starting point. Schedule it as a saved search (typically every 5–15 minutes over a rolling lookback equal to the alert's intended detection window). Tune the threshold (`where`/`stats` clauses) to your environment's normal baseline before enabling alert actions. For high-volume sources, use `tstats` against the accelerated data model when possible.

Step 5 — Troubleshoot

Common failure modes for this use case:

• **No events arriving** — Confirm the upstream input on the forwarder or HEC endpoint is enabled and reachable from the data-collection tier. Inspect `$SPLUNK_HOME/var/log/splunk/splunkd.log` for input errors. Cross-check with `| tstats count where index=power sourcetype=snmp:apc:ups earliest=-1h`.

• **Field extraction returning null** — Inspect the relevant `props.conf` / `transforms.conf` for the sourcetype on the search head and indexer. A vendor TA upgrade or a corporate hardening script can break the regex. Compare against the TA's default stanza using `splunk btool props list --debug | grep snmp:apc:ups`.

• **Search returns no rows even when the condition is present** — The role running the search may lack `srchIndexesAllowed` for the underlying index. Run `| rest splunk_server=local /servicesNS/-/-/authorization/roles | search title=`role_name` | table title srchIndexesAllowed`, replacing the role name with the role that owns the saved search.

• **High false-positive rate** — Maintain an exception lookup keyed on the dominant noise field (host, user, src, process_name, etc.) and join it to the alert with `| lookup <exceptions>.csv key OUTPUT in_exceptions | where in_exceptions!="yes"`. Prefer narrow per-key suppressions over wholesale disabling.

• **Alert fires repeatedly during expected maintenance windows** — Maintain a `maintenance_windows` lookup and join it against the alert: `| lookup maintenance_windows host OUTPUT in_window | where in_window!="yes"`. Keep the lookup in source control next to the saved-search definitions.

• **Alert never fires even when the dashboard shows the condition** — The alert's scheduled time range probably doesn't match the search. Verify cron schedule and earliest/latest tokens align with the intended detection window.
